articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, Designates International Criminal Court Officials, and Removes Burma-Related Designation
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics. Concurrently, OFAC designated officials associated with the International Criminal Court (ICC) and issued related General Licenses.

In a separate action, OFAC also removed a designation related to Burma, indicating a shift in sanctions policy concerning certain entities in the region. These actions reflect OFAC's ongoing efforts to enforce sanctions while also making targeted adjustments to its programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued a new General License pertaining to Russia. This license aims to authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under existing Russia-related sanctions programs.

The issuance of new General Licenses often indicates a refinement of sanctions policy, allowing for specific activities to proceed while maintaining broader restrictions. Details of the authorized activities are available in the full text of the General License.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations, Issues Iran-Related General License, and Amends Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting entities and individuals connected to Iran. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter Iran's destabilizing activities.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued a new Iran-related General License, which may permit certain humanitarian or other specific transactions. Additionally, an existing Russia-related General License has been amended, signaling adjustments to the scope of authorized activities concerning Russia.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes and Updates Designations, Publishes Iran-Related Alert and Amended FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced several designations removals and updates, indicating a recalibration of its sanctions lists. These changes reflect ongoing assessments of sanctioned entities and individuals.

Furthermore, OFAC published a new Iran-related Alert and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). These publications aim to provide updated guidance and highlight potential risks associated with transactions involving Iran.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations under its counter-terrorism sanctions program. These actions target individuals and entities identified as supporting terrorist activities globally.

These designations aim to disrupt financial networks and limit the ability of terrorist organizations to operate. The specific details of the designated parties and the reasons for their inclusion are outlined in OFAC's official announcement.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Issues Determination and Amended FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has imposed new designations targeting entities and individuals linked to Iran, alongside designations against transnational criminal organizations. These actions underscore OFAC's commitment to combating illicit financial activities.

In addition to the designations, OFAC published an Iran-related Determination and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). These documents provide further clarity and guidance regarding the scope and implementation of Iran sanctions.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Counter Terrorism and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Removes Belarus, Counter Narcotics, and Libya Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting entities involved in counter-terrorism and transnational criminal organizations. These actions aim to disrupt illicit networks and safeguard the international financial system.

Concurrently, OFAC removed several designations related to Belarus, counter narcotics efforts, and Libya. These removals suggest a reassessment of certain sanctions targets and may indicate evolving geopolitical considerations.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Narcotics, Counter Terrorism, Iran-Related, and Non-Proliferation Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a series of new designations across multiple sanctions programs. These include actions targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics, counter terrorism, Iran-related activities, and non-proliferation efforts.

These comprehensive designations highlight OFAC's multi-faceted approach to combating various threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. The actions aim to disrupt illicit networks and prevent the proliferation of dangerous weapons.

articles.headline: OFAC Publishes Regulatory Amendments, Cuba Sanctions Regulations, New and Amended Cuba-Related FAQs, and Cuba-Related Alert
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has published significant regulatory amendments, including updates to the Cuba Sanctions Regulations. These changes reflect ongoing adjustments to U.S. policy towards Cuba.

In addition to the regulatory updates, OFAC issued new and amended Cuba-related Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) and a Cuba-related Alert. These resources aim to provide clarity and guidance to the public regarding the updated sanctions framework and potential compliance considerations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Venezuela General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued amended General Licenses pertaining to Venezuela. These amendments modify existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Venezuela, which would otherwise be prohibited under U.S. sanctions.

The issuance of amended General Licenses often signifies a recalibration of sanctions policy, potentially easing or tightening restrictions on specific sectors or activities. The full details of the changes are available in the updated General Licenses.

Details of the specific violations leading to this penalty are outlined in the settlement agreement. OFAC continues to emphasize the importance of robust compliance programs for all entities engaged in international trade and finance to prevent sanctions breaches.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $1,427,230 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations

This significant penalty underscores OFAC's commitment to enforcing sanctions against individuals as well as corporations.

The enforcement action highlights the personal responsibility individuals bear in adhering to sanctions compliance. The specific nature of the violations leading to this substantial fine is detailed in OFAC's enforcement release.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Faces Massive $275,000,000 OFAC Penalty
body: Adani Enterprises Limited has been assessed an unprecedented civil monetary penalty of $275,000,000 by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This colossal fine represents one of the largest penalties ever levied by OFAC, highlighting the severe consequences of sanctions violations.

The enforcement action against such a prominent international entity sends a strong message about OFAC's resolve to enforce U.S. sanctions laws globally. Companies of all sizes are urged to review and strengthen their compliance frameworks to avoid similar penalties.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Civil Money Penalty Against American Express National Bank for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has announced a cease-and-desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank (AENB) for significant deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program. The OCC found that AENB failed to establish and maintain a BSA/AML compliance program reasonably designed to assure and monitor compliance with the BSA and its implementing regulations.

Deficiencies identified in AENB's program included inadequate resources, such as staff lacking sufficient expertise, systemic internal control gaps, weak independent testing, and insufficient BSA/AML training for employees and directors. The bank also failed to adequately tailor its BSA/AML risk assessment to its business activities, focusing too narrowly on demand deposit accounts and not enough on the risks associated with its more dominant credit and charge card products.

These failures led to systemic breakdowns in suspicious activity monitoring and reporting, resulting in the bank's inability to timely identify, evaluate, and sufficiently report approximately $13 billion of suspected trade-based money laundering activity over the past decade. The OCC emphasized that banks of American Express's size and complexity are expected to devote sufficient resources to detect and prevent money laundering, which is crucial for both economic and national security.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
